claims.text: Near-equiatomic multi-element alloys have high configurational or mixing entropy.
High configurational entropy thermodynamically favors a uniform random solid-solution phase over intermetallic formation.
The high-temperature stability of near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles is governed by a balance between configurational entropy and differential elemental diffusion.
Reducing the proportion of fast-diffusing elements produces more effective diffusion barriers, especially at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary and intraparticle diffusion barriers impede phase segregation and high-temperature degradation.
The distribution of fast- and slow-diffusing elements dictates the formation and integrity of diffusion barriers within the nanoparticles.
A lower fraction of fast-diffusing elements mitigates localized atomic rearrangement and diffusion.
An excess of fast-diffusing elements permits rapid rearrangement that can overcome configurational-entropy stabilization.
Rapid rearrangement caused by excess fast-diffusing elements triggers secondary-phase segregation and degradation of the uniform solid solution.
Reducing fast-diffusing-element content should yield a more uniform microstructure than a strictly equiatomic baseline after high-temperature exposure.
Reducing fast-diffusing-element content should reduce phase segregation and better preserve composition during high-temperature exposure.
Increasing fast-diffusing-element content should accelerate degradation and secondary-phase formation.
The proposed mechanism applies across catalytic temperatures of 773–1173 K and thermoelectric temperatures of 473–1923 K.
Surface diffusion plays a significant role under the specified controlled reactive or inert atmospheres.
Very high or low pressures and unconventional reactive atmospheres can alter diffusion kinetics enough to invalidate the proposed relationship.

contradictions.description: The intervention and experimental design specify only an equiatomic baseline and a reduced-fast-diffuser group, but the prediction and falsification rule also require testing a group with increased fast-diffusing-element content. That required comparison is absent from the stated design.
